### Task 1: CBSA Population Breakdown
I initially attempted to use the 2024 ACS one-year estimates, but the selected Korean population variable returned missing values. I switched to the 2024 ACS five-year estimates to obtain the required population data.

```{r}
# Load required packages
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)

# Create the folder for cached data
dir.create("data/mp03", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Define population variables
population_variables <- c(
  korean = "B02018_005",
  total = "B01003_001"
)

# PART A: Download and cache ACS-1 data

acs1_file <- "data/mp03/cbsa_population_acs1.csv"

if (!file.exists(acs1_file)) {
  cbsa_acs1 <- get_acs(
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = population_variables,
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs1"
  )

  write_csv(cbsa_acs1, acs1_file)
}

cbsa_acs1 <- read_csv(
  acs1_file,
  col_types = cols(GEOID = col_character())
)

# Check availability of ACS-1 population estimates
acs1_check <- cbsa_acs1 |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(
    available = sum(!is.na(estimate)),
    missing = sum(is.na(estimate)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# PART B: Download and cache ACS-5 data

acs5_file <- "data/mp03/cbsa_population_acs5.csv"

if (!file.exists(acs5_file)) {
  cbsa_acs5 <- get_acs(
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = population_variables,
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5"
  )

  write_csv(cbsa_acs5, acs5_file)
}

cbsa_acs5 <- read_csv(
  acs5_file,
  col_types = cols(GEOID = col_character())
)


# PART C: Prepare ACS-5 population data

cbsa_summary <- cbsa_acs5 |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = estimate
  ) |>
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = 100 * korean / total
  )


# PART D: Explore Korean American populations

# Top 10 areas by Korean American population
top_korean_cbsa <- cbsa_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(korean), !is.na(total), total > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(korean)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

top_korean_cbsa |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "CBSA Code",
      "Metropolitan or Micropolitan Area",
      "Total Population",
      "Korean Population",
      "Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Top 10 Areas by Korean American Population"
  )

# Top 10 areas by Korean American population percentage
top_korean_percentage <- cbsa_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(korean_percentage), total > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(korean_percentage)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

top_korean_percentage |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "CBSA Code",
      "Metropolitan or Micropolitan Area",
      "Total Population",
      "Korean Population",
      "Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Top 10 Areas by Korean American Population Percentage"
  )
```


### Task 2: NYC Tract Population Breakdown

```{r}
# TASK 2: NYC CENSUS TRACT POPULATION BREAKDOWN

# Load required packages
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Create the data folder if it does not exist
dir.create("data/mp03", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Define the five NYC boroughs using county FIPS codes
nyc_counties <- c("005", "047", "061", "081", "085")

# Define the Census variables
tract_variables <- c(
  korean = "B02018_005",
  total = "B01003_001"
)

# Define the cached geographic data file
tract_file <- "data/mp03/nyc_tract_population.gpkg"

# Download only if the file does not already exist
if (!file.exists(tract_file)) {

  nyc_tracts <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = tract_variables,
    state = "NY",
    county = nyc_counties,
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    geometry = TRUE,
    output = "wide"
  )

  # Save the geographic data and population estimates
  st_write(nyc_tracts, tract_file, quiet = TRUE)
}

# Read the saved geographic data
nyc_tracts <- st_read(tract_file, quiet = TRUE)

# Calculate Korean American population percentage
nyc_tracts <- nyc_tracts |>
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = if_else(
      totalE > 0,
      100 * koreanE / totalE,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

# Display a summary of the census tract data
data.frame(
  Metric = "NYC Census Tracts",
  Count = nrow(nyc_tracts)
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "NYC Census Tract Data Summary",
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )
```


### Task 3: NYC Neighborhood Tabulation Areas

```{r}
# TASK 3: DOWNLOAD AND LOAD NYC NTA SHAPEFILE

library(sf)

# Function to download, extract, and load NYC NTA data
load_nyc_nta <- function() {

  # Create the data directory
  data_dir <- "data/mp03"

  dir.create(
    data_dir,
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = FALSE
  )

  # Define file locations
  zip_file <- file.path(data_dir, "nynta2020_26d.zip")
  unzip_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "nyc_nta")

  # NYC Department of City Planning download URL
  nta_url <- paste0(
    "https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/dcp/assets/files/",
    "zip/data-tools/bytes/nynta2020_26d.zip"
  )

  # Check whether the ZIP file is already cached
  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) {

    # Use the file previously downloaded to the computer
    local_zip <- "C:/Users/hannatu/Downloads/nynta2020_26d.zip"

    if (file.exists(local_zip)) {

      file.copy(
        from = local_zip,
        to = zip_file
      )

    } else {

      # Download from NYC if no local copy exists
      download.file(
        url = nta_url,
        destfile = zip_file,
        mode = "wb"
      )
    }
  }

  # Find any previously extracted shapefile
  shp_files <- list.files(
    path = unzip_dir,
    pattern = "\\.shp$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE
  )

  # Extract the ZIP if the shapefile is not present
  if (length(shp_files) == 0) {

    dir.create(
      unzip_dir,
      recursive = TRUE,
      showWarnings = FALSE
    )

    unzip(
      zipfile = zip_file,
      exdir = unzip_dir
    )

    shp_files <- list.files(
      path = unzip_dir,
      pattern = "\\.shp$",
      recursive = TRUE,
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  }

  # Stop if no shapefile is found
  if (length(shp_files) == 0) {
    stop("NTA shapefile was not found.")
  }

  # Read the NTA shapefile as an sf object
  nta_data <- st_read(
    shp_files[1],
    quiet = TRUE
  )

  # Keep the columns needed for neighborhood analysis
  nta_data <- nta_data |>
    select(
      NTA2020,
      NTAName,
      BoroName
    )

  # Return the geographic data
  return(nta_data)
}


# LOAD AND CHECK THE NYC NTA DATA
nyc_nta <- load_nyc_nta()
# Display a summary of the neighborhood data
data.frame(
  Metric = "Neighborhood Tabulation Areas",
  Count = nrow(nyc_nta)
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "NYC Neighborhood Data Summary",
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )


```


### Task 4: Aggregate Census Tract Data to Neighborhoods

```{r}
# TASK 4: AGGREGATE CENSUS TRACTS TO NTAs

library(sf)
library(dplyr)

# Check that both datasets are available
stopifnot(
  inherits(nyc_tracts, "sf"),
  inherits(nyc_nta, "sf")
)

# Make sure both datasets use the same coordinate system
nyc_tracts <- st_transform(nyc_tracts, st_crs(nyc_nta))

# Assign each census tract to the NTA with the largest overlap
tract_nta_join <- st_join(
  nyc_tracts,
  nyc_nta %>% select(NTA2020),
  largest = TRUE,
  left = TRUE
)

# Check how many tracts were matched


# Remove geometry and aggregate population estimates
nta_population <- tract_nta_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(NTA2020)) %>%
  group_by(NTA2020) %>%
  summarise(
    korean_population = sum(
      koreanE,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    total_population = sum(
      totalE,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = if_else(
      total_population > 0,
      100 * korean_population / total_population,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

# Join population results back to neighborhood boundaries
nyc_nta_population <- nyc_nta %>%
  left_join(
    nta_population,
    by = "NTA2020"
  )


# Check the number of neighborhoods


# Find the 10 neighborhoods with the largest Korean population
nyc_nta_population %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(korean_population)) %>%
  select(
    NTAName,
    BoroName,
    korean_population,
    korean_percentage
  ) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Neighborhood",
      "Borough",
      "Korean Population",
      "Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Top 10 NYC Neighborhoods by Korean American Population"
  )
```


### Task 5: Download and Cache NYC PLUTO Data

```{r}
# TASK 5: DOWNLOAD NYC PLUTO DATA USING PAGINATION

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# Function to download and cache the complete NYC PLUTO dataset
load_nyc_pluto <- function() {

  # STEP 1: Create the folder for PLUTO data

  data_dir <- "data/mp03/pluto"

  dir.create(
    data_dir,
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = FALSE
  )

  # Location of the final cached dataset
  cache_file <- file.path(data_dir, "nyc_pluto.rds")

  # STEP 2: Check for an existing complete dataset

  if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
    message("Loading cached NYC PLUTO data...")
    return(readRDS(cache_file))
  }

  # STEP 3: Define the NYC Open Data API

  base_url <- paste0(
    "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/",
    "64uk-42ks.csv"
  )

  # Number of records per request
  batch_size <- 10000

  # Starting record
  offset <- 0

  # STEP 4: Download the data in batches

  repeat {

    # Prevent scientific notation in the API URL
    offset_text <- format(
      offset,
      scientific = FALSE,
      trim = TRUE
    )

    # Create the API request URL
    request_url <- paste0(
      base_url,
      "?$limit=", batch_size,
      "&$offset=", offset_text,
      "&$order=bbl"
    )

    # File for the current batch
    batch_file <- file.path(
      data_dir,
      paste0("pluto_batch_", offset_text, ".csv")
    )

    # Download only if the batch is not already cached
    if (!file.exists(batch_file)) {

      message("Downloading records starting at ", offset_text)

      # Download to a temporary file first
      temp_file <- paste0(batch_file, ".tmp")

      tryCatch({

        download.file(
          url = request_url,
          destfile = temp_file,
          mode = "wb",
          quiet = TRUE
        )

        # Check that the download created a file
        if (!file.exists(temp_file)) {
          stop("Download did not create a file.")
        }

        # Move the completed download into the cache
        if (!file.rename(temp_file, batch_file)) {
          stop("Could not save the downloaded batch.")
        }

      }, error = function(e) {

        # Remove an incomplete temporary download
        if (file.exists(temp_file)) {
          file.remove(temp_file)
        }

        stop(
          "Download failed at offset ",
          offset_text,
          ": ",
          conditionMessage(e)
        )
      })
    }

    # STEP 5: Read the current batch

    batch <- read_csv(
      batch_file,
      col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
      show_col_types = FALSE,
      progress = FALSE
    )

    batch_rows <- nrow(batch)

    message(
      "Batch at offset ",
      offset_text,
      ": ",
      batch_rows,
      " records"
    )

    # An empty batch means there are no more records
    if (batch_rows == 0) {
      break
    }

    # Stop after the final partial batch
    if (batch_rows < batch_size) {
      break
    }

    # Move to the next batch
    offset <- offset + batch_size
  }

  # STEP 6: Find all downloaded batch files

  batch_files <- list.files(
    data_dir,
    pattern = "^pluto_batch_[0-9]+\\.csv$",
    full.names = TRUE
  )

  # Sort batches by their numeric offsets
  batch_offsets <- as.numeric(
    sub(
      "^pluto_batch_([0-9]+)\\.csv$",
      "\\1",
      basename(batch_files)
    )
  )

  batch_files <- batch_files[order(batch_offsets)]

  # STEP 7: Combine all batches into one dataset

  message("Combining downloaded PLUTO batches...")

  pluto_data <- bind_rows(
    lapply(batch_files, function(file) {

      read_csv(
        file,
        col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
        show_col_types = FALSE,
        progress = FALSE
      )
    })
  )

  # STEP 8: Save the complete dataset locally

  saveRDS(
    object = pluto_data,
    file = cache_file
  )

  message("NYC PLUTO data downloaded and cached successfully!")

  return(pluto_data)
}


# STEP 9: LOAD THE COMPLETE NYC PLUTO DATASET

nyc_pluto <- load_nyc_pluto()
```

## Task 6: Exploratory Data Analysis

### Question 1: Which NYC census tract has the most office floor area?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)

# Convert office area into numeric values
pluto_office <- nyc_pluto %>%
  mutate(
    officearea = parse_number(officearea)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bct2020),
    bct2020 != ""
  )

# Add together the office floor area for each census tract
office_by_tract <- pluto_office %>%
  group_by(bct2020) %>%
  summarise(
    total_office_area = sum(
      officearea,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_office_area))

# Display the top 10 census tracts
office_by_tract %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Census Tract ID",
      "Total Office Area (sq. ft.)"
    ),
    caption = "Top 10 NYC Census Tracts by Office Floor Area",
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )

# Identify the tract with the largest office area
top_office_tract <- office_by_tract %>%
  slice_max(
    total_office_area,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

```

### Question 2: Which NYC Neighborhood Has the Most Residential Units?

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)

# Select PLUTO properties with valid coordinates
pluto_residential <- nyc_pluto %>%
  mutate(
    latitude = parse_number(latitude),
    longitude = parse_number(longitude),
    unitsres = parse_number(unitsres)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(latitude),
    !is.na(longitude),
    !is.na(unitsres),
    unitsres >= 0
  )

# Convert property locations into geographic points
pluto_points <- st_as_sf(
  pluto_residential,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = TRUE
)

# Match coordinate systems
pluto_points <- st_transform(
  pluto_points,
  st_crs(nyc_nta)
)

# Assign each property to its neighborhood
pluto_nta_join <- st_join(
  pluto_points,
  nyc_nta %>%
    select(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName),
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

# Calculate total residential units by neighborhood
residential_by_nta <- pluto_nta_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(NTA2020)) %>%
  group_by(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName) %>%
  summarise(
    residential_units = sum(unitsres, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(residential_units))

# Display the 10 neighborhoods with the most residential units
residential_by_nta %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "NTA Code",
      "Neighborhood",
      "Borough",
      "Residential Units"
    ),
    caption = "Top 10 NYC Neighborhoods by Residential Units",
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )

# Identify the neighborhood with the most residential units
top_residential_nta <- residential_by_nta %>%
  slice_head(n = 1)
```

### Question 3: Which NYC Census Tract Has the Highest Population per Residential Square Foot or Unit?
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(sf)
library(knitr)

# Convert PLUTO tract IDs to Census GEOIDs
pluto_with_geoid <- nyc_pluto %>%
  mutate(
    borough_code = substr(bct2020, 1, 1),
    tract_code = substr(bct2020, 2, 7),
    county_code = case_when(
      borough_code == "1" ~ "061",
      borough_code == "2" ~ "005",
      borough_code == "3" ~ "047",
      borough_code == "4" ~ "081",
      borough_code == "5" ~ "085",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    GEOID = if_else(
      !is.na(county_code) &
        grepl("^[0-9]{6}$", tract_code),
      paste0("36", county_code, tract_code),
      NA_character_
    )
  )

# Aggregate residential floor area and units by tract
residential_by_tract <- pluto_with_geoid %>%
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) %>%
  mutate(
    resarea = parse_number(resarea),
    unitsres = parse_number(unitsres)
  ) %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarise(
    total_residential_area = sum(resarea, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_residential_units = sum(unitsres, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Combine population and residential data
tract_density <- nyc_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, totalE) %>%
  left_join(residential_by_tract, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    population_per_sqft = if_else(
      !is.na(total_residential_area) &
        total_residential_area > 0,
      totalE / total_residential_area,
      NA_real_
    ),
    population_per_unit = if_else(
      !is.na(total_residential_units) &
        total_residential_units > 0,
      totalE / total_residential_units,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

# Top five tracts by population per residential square foot
top_density_sqft <- tract_density %>%
  filter(!is.na(population_per_sqft), totalE > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(population_per_sqft)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_density_sqft %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, population_per_sqft) %>%
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Highest Population per Residential Square Foot"
  )

# Top five tracts by population per residential unit
top_density_units <- tract_density %>%
  filter(!is.na(population_per_unit), totalE > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(population_per_unit)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_density_units %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, population_per_unit) %>%
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Highest Population per Residential Unit"
  )

# Sensitivity check: tracts with at least 100 residential units
density_check <- tract_density %>%
  filter(
    total_residential_units >= 100,
    total_residential_area > 0,
    totalE > 0
  )

# Highest-ranked tract under each measure after filtering
density_check %>%
  arrange(desc(population_per_sqft)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, population_per_sqft) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Population per Square Foot: 100+ Residential Units"
  )

density_check %>%
  arrange(desc(population_per_unit)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, population_per_unit) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Population per Unit: 100+ Residential Units"
  )
```
The original result showed an unusually high value of 794 people per residential unit, but Census tracts with very few recorded residential units can produce extreme ratios. I applied a minimum threshold of 100 residential units to reduce the influence of small denominators, and the filtered result of 21.65 people per unit may still reflect data limitations.

### Question 4: Which Five Metropolitan Areas Have the Highest Korean American Population Share?

```{r}
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Download 2024 ACS 5-year metropolitan-area data
metro_acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "cbsa",
  variables = c(
    korean = "B02018_005",
    total = "B01003_001"
  ),
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

# Calculate Korean American population percentages
metro_korean <- metro_acs %>%
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = koreanE / totalE * 100
  )

# Exclude NYC and micropolitan areas
top5_korean_metros <- metro_korean %>%
  filter(
    grepl("Metro Area", NAME),
    !grepl("New York-Newark-Jersey City", NAME),
    !is.na(korean_percentage),
    totalE > 0
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(korean_percentage)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

# Display the top five metropolitan areas
top5_korean_metros %>%
  select(NAME, koreanE, totalE, korean_percentage) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Metropolitan Area",
      "Korean Population",
      "Total Population",
      "Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Top Five Metropolitan Areas by Korean American Population Share"
  )
```

### Question 5: Geographic Distribution of Korean Americans in Los Angeles

```{r}
library(tidycensus)
library(tigris)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

# Download Korean American population data by census tract
la_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    korean = "B02018_005",
    total = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "CA",
  county = "Los Angeles",
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5",
  geometry = TRUE,
  output = "wide"
)

# Download California Census Place boundaries
ca_places <- places(
  state = "CA",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
)

# Identify places intersecting Los Angeles County
la_county_boundary <- st_union(la_tracts)

la_places <- ca_places %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(la_tracts)) %>%
  st_filter(la_county_boundary)

# Keep place identifiers and names
la_places_simple <- la_places %>%
  select(
    place_geoid = GEOID,
    place_name = NAME
  )

# Assign each census tract to its largest-overlapping place
la_tract_places <- st_join(
  la_tracts,
  la_places_simple,
  join = st_intersects,
  left = TRUE,
  largest = TRUE
)

# Calculate Korean American population by place
la_place_population <- la_tract_places %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(place_geoid)) %>%
  group_by(place_geoid, place_name) %>%
  summarise(
    korean_population = sum(koreanE, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_population = sum(totalE, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = if_else(
      total_population > 0,
      korean_population / total_population * 100,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(korean_population))

# Table: Top 10 places by Korean American population
la_place_population %>%
  select(
    place_name,
    korean_population,
    total_population,
    korean_percentage
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Place",
      "Korean Population",
      "Total Population",
      "Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Top 10 Los Angeles County Places by Korean American Population"
  )

# Join population estimates to place boundaries
la_map <- la_places %>%
  left_join(
    la_place_population,
    by = c("GEOID" = "place_geoid")
  )

# Map: Korean American population share
ggplot(la_map) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = korean_percentage),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma",
    na.value = "grey90",
    name = "Korean\npopulation (%)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Korean American Population in LA County",
    subtitle = "Estimated percentage by Census Place",
    caption = "Source: 2024 ACS 5-Year Estimates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```


### Question 6: What Percentage of Korean Americans Live in Major U.S. Metropolitan Areas?

```{r}
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Get the nationwide Korean American population
us_korean <- get_acs(
  geography = "us",
  variables = c(
    korean = "B02018_005",
    total = "B01003_001"
  ),
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

# Nationwide Korean American population
us_korean_total <- us_korean$koreanE[1]

# Calculate each metropolitan area's share of the national total
metro_national_share <- metro_korean %>%
  filter(grepl("Metro Area", NAME)) %>%
  mutate(
    share_of_us_koreans = koreanE / us_korean_total * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(koreanE))

# Display the top 10 metropolitan areas
metro_national_share %>%
  select(NAME, koreanE, share_of_us_koreans) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Metropolitan Area",
      "Korean Population",
      "Share of U.S. Korean Population (%)"
    ),
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Korean American Population in Major U.S. Metropolitan Areas"
  )

# Calculate New York metropolitan area's share
ny_metro_share <- metro_national_share %>%
  filter(grepl("New York-Newark-Jersey City", NAME)) %>%
  select(NAME, koreanE, share_of_us_koreans)


```

### Question 7: Relationship Between Population and Residential Units

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Prepare NYC census tract housing and population data
housing_relationship <- tract_density %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(totalE),
    !is.na(total_residential_units),
    total_residential_units > 0,
    totalE > 0
  )

# Calculate correlation
housing_correlation <- cor(
  housing_relationship$total_residential_units,
  housing_relationship$totalE
)

# Fit linear regression model
housing_model <- lm(
  totalE ~ total_residential_units,
  data = housing_relationship
)

# Calculate R-squared
housing_r_squared <- summary(housing_model)$r.squared

# Display numerical results
cat("Correlation:", round(housing_correlation, 3), "\n")
cat("R-squared:", round(housing_r_squared, 3), "\n")

# Create scatterplot with regression line
ggplot(
  housing_relationship,
  aes(x = total_residential_units, y = totalE)
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.3,
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population vs. Residential Units in NYC",
    subtitle = "Relationship across NYC census tracts",
    x = "Number of Residential Units",
    y = "Census Tract Population",
    caption = "Sources: 2024 ACS 5-Year Estimates and NYC PLUTO"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


### Question 8: Which NYC Neighborhoods Have the Tallest Buildings?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(sf)
library(knitr)

# Prepare building floor counts from PLUTO
building_floors <- pluto_nta_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(NTA2020)) %>%
  mutate(
    numfloors = parse_number(numfloors)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(numfloors),
    numfloors > 0
  )

# Identify unusually high floor counts
building_floors %>%
  filter(numfloors > 120) %>%
  select(address, NTAName, BoroName, numfloors) %>%
  arrange(desc(numfloors)) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Building Records Exceeding 120 Floors"
  )

# Apply exploratory cutoff of 120 floors
tallest_by_nta_clean <- building_floors %>%
  filter(numfloors <= 120) %>%
  group_by(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName) %>%
  summarise(
    tallest_building_floors = max(numfloors),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(tallest_building_floors))

# Display the top 10 NTAs
tallest_by_nta_clean %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  select(
    NTAName,
    BoroName,
    tallest_building_floors
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Neighborhood",
      "Borough",
      "Maximum Recorded Floors"
    ),
    caption = "Top 10 NYC NTAs by Maximum Building Floors"
  )
```
The PLUTO dataset contains an unusually high floor-count value of 342.87. I excluded records above 120 floors as an exploratory data-cleaning decision. The ranking therefore reflects the filtered dataset, not necessarily the definitive tallest buildings in NYC.

### Question 10: How Many New Yorkers Live in Primarily Commercial Areas?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)

# Calculate commercial and residential floor space by tract
commercial_by_tract <- pluto_with_geoid %>%
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) %>%
  mutate(
    comarea = parse_number(comarea),
    resarea = parse_number(resarea)
  ) %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarise(
    total_commercial_area = sum(comarea, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_residential_area = sum(resarea, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Join floor space to census tract population
commercial_population <- nyc_tracts %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, totalE) %>%
  left_join(commercial_by_tract, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    primarily_commercial = total_commercial_area >
      total_residential_area
  )

# Summarize population in primarily commercial tracts
commercial_summary <- commercial_population %>%
  filter(primarily_commercial %in% TRUE) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_tracts = n(),
    population = sum(totalE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Display the results
commercial_summary %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Number of Commercial-Dominant Tracts",
      "Estimated Population"
    ),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    caption = "Population Living in Commercial-Dominant NYC Census Tracts"
  )
```
## Task 7: Korean Americans in the United States

### Korean American Population Distribution in NYC

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Calculate Korean American population percentage
nyc_korean_map <- nyc_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    korean_percentage = if_else(
      !is.na(totalE) & totalE > 0,
      koreanE / totalE * 100,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

# Create NYC Korean American population map
ggplot(nyc_korean_map) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = korean_percentage),
    color = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma",

    name = "Korean\npopulation (%)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Korean American Population Across NYC",
    subtitle = "Percentage of residents by census tract",
    caption = "Source: 2024 ACS 5-Year Estimates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
### Written Analysis

About 2,062,223 Korean Americans live across the United States out of 334,922,499 people total. While Korean Americans live in many states, they aren't spread evenly across the map. Larger groups tend to show up in major metro areas, where jobs, family ties, and established communities are often discussed as key influences on settlement. Looking at where people live helps show how these communities take shape and why certain places hold larger populations over time.

Based on 2024 ACS 5 year estimates, Los Angeles has the largest Korean American population at 343,006 people (16.63% of the national total), followed by New York–Newark–Jersey City at 225,542 (10.94%) and Washington, DC at 108,241 (5.25%). Together, Los Angeles and New York make up 27.57% of Korean Americans nationwide. Still, raw counts tell a different story than local shares. Urban Honolulu has fewer Korean Americans (42,534) than Los Angeles, yet they make up 4.25% of Honolulu's total population compared to 2.64% in Los Angeles.

Local maps show how communities spread out within a region rather than sitting in just one spot. Across Los Angeles County, approximate place level estimates created by assigning each census tract to its largest overlapping Census Place put the City of Los Angeles highest in headcount at 113,594 residents (2.94% of the city), while suburban places often show higher local shares, such as Cerritos at 11.79% (5,643 people), La Mirada at 11.28% (5,323), and Torrance at 8.61% (12,243). In New York City, neighborhood data points to strong clustering in Queens led by Murray Hill Broadway Flushing with about 7,944 Korean American residents and the NYC map shows that certain census tracts in northeastern Queens, especially around Flushing, reach much higher Korean American population percentages than most other parts of the city.

Historical context on Korean immigrants distinct from the Census estimates for the overall Korean American population, which includes U.S. born residents helps explain why these hubs grew. Research on Korean immigrants notes that the 1965 immigration law led to larger waves of Korean arrivals, with many settling in places like California and New York alongside family connections and major metro opportunities (Esterline & Batalova, 2022). Over time, local churches and community institutions helped support families and newcomers across urban centers and suburbs (Zhou & Kim, 2007). While census numbers alone can't prove why individuals choose specific places, pairing them with historical research gives a fuller picture of how migration history and community networks align with today's geographic patterns.

### References

- Esterline, C., & Batalova, J. (2022, April 14). *Korean Immigrants in the United States*. Migration Policy Institute. https://www.migrationpolicy.org/journal/spotlight/korean-immigrants-united-states-2022

- Zhou, M., & Kim, S. S. (2007, May 3). *After-School Institutions in Chinese and Korean Immigrant Communities: A Model for Others?* Migration Policy Institute. https://platform.migrationpolicy.org/article/after-school-institutions-chinese-and-korean-immigrant-communities-model-others
